Compute IDM Cut Scores Using MAPT-Style Logistic Regressions

computeCutsIDMMAPT.Rd

Finds cut scores from item difficulties and raters' assignments of items to ordered performance levels. A cut score is a position on the item-difficulty scale, such as 500. For each boundary between levels, the function fits a logistic curve to all available ratings together. The cut is where that curve reaches probability 0.5. This provides a MAPT-style comparison with the moving-average method in computeCutsIDM.

Usage

computeCutsIDMMAPT(
  dat,
  boundaries = c(1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5),
  est_col = "est",
  item_id_col = NULL,
  rater_cols = NULL,
  rater_pattern = "Rater",
  rater_id_col = NULL,
  rating_col = NULL,
  input_format = c("auto", "long", "wide"),
  rating_levels = NULL,
  missing = c("drop", "error"),
  cut_labels = NULL,
  per_rater = TRUE
)

Arguments

dat

A data frame with item difficulty estimates and ratings.

boundaries

Boundaries on the rating-index scale, in increasing order. Use half-integers, for example c(1.5, 2.5) for three levels. These numbers select which levels to separate; they are not item difficulties or the resulting cut scores. If omitted and rating_levels is supplied, all adjacent boundaries are used. See the label example below.

est_col

Name of the numeric item-difficulty column. The returned cut scores use this same scale. All values must be finite and nonmissing.

item_id_col

Name of the item identifier column. Required for long input; optional for wide input, where rows otherwise identify items.

rater_cols

Names of the rating columns in wide input. If NULL, they are selected using rater_pattern.

rater_pattern

Regular expression used to select wide rating columns when rater_cols is NULL.

rater_id_col

Name of the rater identifier column in long input.

rating_col

Name of the rating column in long input.

input_format

Input layout. Long input requires item_id_col, rater_id_col, and rating_col. Wide input has one row per item and one column per rater. "auto" infers the layout from the supplied column arguments.

rating_levels

Optional vector of rating labels, listed from lowest to highest level. For example, c("1a", "1b", "2", "3", "4"). Their positions in this vector become indices 1, ..., K, where K is the number of levels. The supplied order determines the order used in the calculation. Without this argument, ratings must be numeric positive integer indices.

missing

"drop" (default) removes missing ratings and keeps the other ratings, including other raters' ratings of the same item. "error" stops if a rating is missing. This option does not remove missing item difficulties or identifiers: these always cause an error.

cut_labels

Optional distinct, nonempty names for the requested cuts. Defaults to names such as cut12 without explicit rating_levels, or cut_1a_1b with explicit category labels. The name "person" is reserved and cannot be used for a cut.

per_rater

TRUE (default) also computes separate models and cuts for each rater, to help compare raters. FALSE computes only the joint result. Either choice gives the same pooled cuts.

Details

1. Start with ordered ratings and item difficulties

Each observation is one rater's rating of one item. In long format, each observation has its own row. In wide format, each item has one row and each rater has a rating column. Each item must have the same difficulty wherever it occurs. An item–rater pair must occur at most once.

The function uses the order of the rating levels. With rating_levels = c("1a", "1b", "2", "3", "4"), the mapping is:

Rating labelIndex used in the calculation
1a1
1b2
23
34
45

For example, boundaries = 3.5 separates indices 3 and 4, so it separates the labels "2" and "3". The resulting cut might be 500 on the item-difficulty scale. The boundary 3.5 and the cut 500 are different quantities.

2. Ask one yes-or-no question per boundary

For each boundary, ask: is this rating above the boundary? Code yes as 1 and no as 0. Let \(i\) identify an item, \(r\) a rater, and \(k\) a requested boundary. Write \(R_{ir}\) for the rating index and \(b_k\) for the boundary. The binary outcome is $$Y_{irk} = \mathbf{1}(R_{ir} > b_k).$$ The symbol \(\mathbf{1}(\cdot)\) means 1 when the condition is true and 0 otherwise. For the boundary between labels "2" and "3", ratings "1a", "1b", and "2" give 0; ratings "3" and "4" give 1.

A separate logistic curve is fitted for each boundary. It describes how the probability of a rating on the upper side changes with item difficulty: $$p_k(x) = \frac{1}{1 + \exp[-(\alpha_k + \beta_k x)]}.$$ Here, \(x\) is item difficulty, \(p_k(x)\) is the fitted probability, \(\alpha_k\) is the intercept, and \(\beta_k\) is the slope. The intercept and slope together determine the curve's position and steepness. The function \(\exp\) is the exponential function. A positive slope means that higher item difficulty goes with a higher probability of a rating above the boundary.

The equivalent logit equation, using the natural logarithm \(\log\), is $$\log\left(\frac{p_k(x)}{1-p_k(x)}\right) = \alpha_k + \beta_k x.$$ The coefficients are estimated by maximum likelihood: the fitted curve is chosen to best account for the observed zeros and ones under this model. This is a probability of a rating-level assignment. It is not the probability that a student answers the item correctly.

3. Find where the curve reaches 0.5

The cut \(c_k\) is the difficulty where the fitted probability is 0.5. At that point, the model gives equal probabilities to ratings on the two sides of the boundary. Since the logit of 0.5 is zero, $$p_k(c_k)=0.5 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \alpha_k + \beta_k c_k = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad c_k = -\frac{\alpha_k}{\beta_k}.$$ For example, an intercept of -10 and a slope of 0.02 give $$c = -\frac{-10}{0.02} = 500.$$ At difficulty 500, the fitted probability is 0.5. There need not be an item with exactly that difficulty, nor exactly half of the observed ratings on each side at that point. The cut comes from the fitted curve.

4. Keep pooled cuts and means of rater cuts separate

The main result is cuts_summary. It contains the cuts from models fitted to all available item–rater observations together. This is called pooling. Each observed rating has equal weight. A rater with more observed ratings therefore contributes more observations; raters are not first reduced to equally weighted summaries. There are no rater-specific intercepts or slopes in the pooled model.

With per_rater = TRUE, the function also repeats the calculation for each rater separately. These cuts are in cuts_per_person. A third table, cuts_summary_per_person, contains their arithmetic means: $$\bar c_k = \frac{1}{m_k}\sum_{r\in V_k} c_{rk}.$$ Here, \(c_{rk}\) is rater \(r\)'s cut for boundary \(k\), \(V_k\) is the set of raters with a finite cut for that boundary, and \(m_k\) is their number. If none is available, the mean is NA.

For example, rater cuts of 480 and 520 have mean 500. The pooled model must still be fitted to the ratings; its cut need not be 500. Fitting a joint curve and averaging separately estimated cuts are different calculations. The mean table is provided for comparison and does not determine cuts_summary.

Use plotCutsIDM(result, show_aggregate = TRUE) to show individual raters and the joint model. The Pooled (MAPT) panel uses cuts_summary. With per_rater = FALSE, the plot shows only that pooled panel, even when show_aggregate = FALSE.

5. Read the diagnostics before interpreting a cut

Start with cut_diagnostics. Its status column explains whether a usable cut was obtained. NA means that no usable cut is available; it does not mean a cut of zero. The corresponding rater information is in diagnostics_per_person.

ok

A finite cut from a converged, increasing curve is available. Also check extrapolated and warning.

no_data

No observed ratings remain for this rater.

one_class

All available ratings are on the same side of this boundary.

constant_est

All available item difficulties are identical.

separation

The difficulty ranges of the zero and one outcomes do not overlap, or only meet at an endpoint. Ordinary logistic regression then has no finite maximum-likelihood slope for this boundary.

nonpositive_slope

The fitted curve decreases or is numerically too flat to supply an acceptable increasing-curve cut.

fit_error, non_convergence, non_finite

The fit failed, did not converge to an acceptable solution, or produced non-finite numerical results. Read the warning column for any further details.

All statuses other than ok give an NA cut. Some diagnostics can also be NA when fitting stopped early.

Extrapolation: a finite cut outside the observed difficulty range is retained, with extrapolated = TRUE. For example, a cut of 700 with items only between 300 and 650 extends beyond the observed items. Treat it more cautiously than a cut within that range.

Order: each boundary has its own model, so the resulting cuts can cross or coincide. cuts_ordered is TRUE only when all pooled cuts are strictly increasing in boundary order. It is FALSE when all are available but not strictly increasing, and NA when any is unavailable. The function does not rearrange cuts to hide this problem.

6. What the calculation does and does not guarantee

This implements the logistic calculation in the MAPT Technical Manual (2006, pp. 54–55). It omits the report's two-pass removal of unusual ratings, so that methods can be compared using unchanged ratings. Each boundary has its own intercept and slope; this is not a proportional-odds model, which would share a slope across boundaries.

No moving average or isotonic regression is applied. Different items may have equal difficulties; there is no need to put tied items in an arbitrary order. This removes that source of order dependence, but it does not make every cut stable. Changed difficulties or ratings can still change a cut; in particular, a shallow curve makes its 0.5 crossing sensitive to changes.

No confidence intervals for cuts are provided. Ordinary standard errors in the stored glm objects do not account for dependence between ratings of the same item or ratings by the same rater. They also do not account for uncertainty in the estimated item difficulties.

Technical note: the scale in stored model objects

For numerical stability, the predictor inside each stored model is $$z = \frac{x-\mu}{s},$$ where \(\mu\) is the mean difficulty and \(s\) is its sample standard deviation over that model's observed rating rows. The model stores these as est_center and est_scale; its predictor column is called difficulty. Thus, predicting from a stored model requires standardized values, not raw est values. The reported diagnostic intercept, slope, and all cut tables are already on the original difficulty scale used in the formulas above. You can use these tables directly.

Value

A list of class cutsIDMMAPT with the following components:

cuts_summary

The main result: a one-row table (tibble) of pooled cuts, with one column per boundary, on the original item-difficulty scale.

cuts_per_person

Auxiliary rater-specific cuts, or NULL when per_rater = FALSE.

cuts_summary_per_person

Arithmetic means of the finite rater-specific cuts, distinct from the pooled result. Unavailable cuts are excluded; a mean is NA if no finite individual cut is available. NULL when per_rater = FALSE.

cut_diagnostics

One row per pooled boundary. cut_name, boundary, and cut identify the requested boundary and resulting cut. n counts rating observations, not unique items; n_lower and n_upper count the zero and one outcomes. intercept and slope are the coefficients on the original difficulty scale. min_est and max_est give the observed range. status, extrapolated, converged, and warning describe fit quality and problems. est_center and est_scale record the numerical standardization described above.

diagnostics_per_person

Diagnostics for each rater, or NULL when per_rater = FALSE.

models

Named list of pooled glm fits; entries may be NULL when a model cannot be fitted.

models_per_person

Named list of raters, each containing a list of glm fits named by cut. Entries may be NULL when a model cannot be fitted. The whole component is NULL when per_rater = FALSE.

data_used

Long-format data used in the models, with columns item_id, person, est, stage_raw, and stage_label.

n_dropped

Number of missing rating observations removed. For wide input this counts missing rating cells; for long input it counts supplied rows with missing ratings.

boundaries, rating_levels, cut_labels, input_format, est_col, item_id_col, rater_id_col, rating_col, missing, method

Settings describing the calculation, input columns, and missing-rating policy.

cuts_ordered

Whether all pooled cuts are strictly increasing in boundary order; NA if any pooled cut is unavailable.

References

Massachusetts Adult Proficiency Tests (MAPT): Technical Manual (2006), pp. 54–55. https://bpb-us-e2.wpmucdn.com/websites.umass.edu/dist/5/40195/files/2021/03/MAPT_TechnicalManualv1.pdf

See also

computeCutsIDM, plotCutsIDM, summary.cutsIDMMAPT, glm

Examples

# Ratings overlap along the difficulty scale, avoiding perfect separation.
dat <- data.frame(
  item = paste0("I", 1:15),
  est = seq(300, 650, length.out = 15),
  Rater1 = c(1, 2, 1, 3, 2, 4, 3, 2, 5, 3, 4, 5, 4, 5, 4),
  Rater2 = c(2, 1, 3, 1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 4, 5, 3, 4, 5, 4, 5)
)
mapt <- computeCutsIDMMAPT(dat, item_id_col = "item")
print(mapt)
#> MAPT pooled binary logistic cuts (no rating trimming)
#> 30 ratings from 2 raters on 15 items; 0 missing ratings dropped.
#> 
#> Pooled cuts (all raters fitted together):
#>  cut_name     cut status extrapolated
#>     cut12 328.096     ok        FALSE
#>     cut23 398.356     ok        FALSE
#>     cut34 487.736     ok        FALSE
#>     cut45 610.108     ok        FALSE
#> 
#> No flagged fits.
#> Extrapolated = cut outside the observed item difficulty range.
#> Individual cuts: summary(x, per_rater = TRUE).
#> Models and ratings remain in the original result: $models, $models_per_person, $data_used.
summary(mapt, per_rater = TRUE)
#> MAPT pooled binary logistic cuts (no rating trimming)
#> 30 ratings from 2 raters on 15 items; 0 missing ratings dropped.
#> 
#> Pooled cuts (all raters fitted together):
#>  cut_name     cut status extrapolated
#>     cut12 328.096     ok        FALSE
#>     cut23 398.356     ok        FALSE
#>     cut34 487.736     ok        FALSE
#>     cut45 610.108     ok        FALSE
#> 
#> No flagged fits.
#> Extrapolated = cut outside the observed item difficulty range.
#> 
#> Individual rater cuts (comparison results):
#>  person   cut12   cut23   cut34   cut45
#>  Rater1 335.468 410.511 487.736 625.158
#>  Rater2 316.552 386.667 487.736 599.188
#> Models and ratings remain in the original result: $models, $models_per_person, $data_used.
# Main result: use the ratings from both raters together.
mapt$cuts_summary
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   cut12 cut23 cut34 cut45
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1  328.  398.  488.  610.
mapt$cut_diagnostics[c("cut_name", "cut", "status", "extrapolated")]
#> # A tibble: 4 × 4
#>   cut_name   cut status extrapolated
#>   <chr>    <dbl> <chr>  <lgl>       
#> 1 cut12     328. ok     FALSE       
#> 2 cut23     398. ok     FALSE       
#> 3 cut34     488. ok     FALSE       
#> 4 cut45     610. ok     FALSE       

# Two different comparison results: individual cuts and their means.
mapt$cuts_per_person
#> # A tibble: 2 × 5
#>   person cut12 cut23 cut34 cut45
#>   <chr>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Rater1  335.  411.  488.  625.
#> 2 Rater2  317.  387.  488.  599.
mapt$cuts_summary_per_person
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   cut12 cut23 cut34 cut45
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1  326.  399.  488.  612.
plotCutsIDM(mapt, show_aggregate = TRUE)


# A hand calculation for an illustrative curve, not the fitted data above:
alpha <- -10
beta <- 0.02
cut <- -alpha / beta                   # 500
1 / (1 + exp(-(alpha + beta * cut)))  # 0.5
#> [1] 0.5

# Compare the same ratings using the moving-average method.
old <- computeCutsIDM(dat)
data.frame(
  method = c("moving_average", "logistic"),
  rbind(old$cuts_summary, mapt$cuts_summary)
)
#>           method    cut12    cut23    cut34    cut45
#> 1 moving_average 319.7917 400.0000 484.3750 606.2500
#> 2       logistic 328.0959 398.3559 487.7358 610.1084

# A complete long-format example with labels 1a, 1b, 2, 3, 4.
level_labels <- c("1a", "1b", "2", "3", "4")
dat_long <- tidyr::pivot_longer(
  dat, cols = c("Rater1", "Rater2"),
  names_to = "Name", values_to = "Kategorie"
)
dat_long$Kategorie <- level_labels[dat_long$Kategorie]
labelled <- computeCutsIDMMAPT(
  dat_long, item_id_col = "item", est_col = "est",
  rater_id_col = "Name", rating_col = "Kategorie", input_format = "long",
  rating_levels = level_labels, missing = "drop"
)
labelled$cuts_summary
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   cut_1a_1b cut_1b_2 cut_2_3 cut_3_4
#>       <dbl>    <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1      328.     398.    488.    610.
plotCutsIDM(labelled, show_aggregate = TRUE)


# Just the boundary between labels "2" and "3" (indices 3 and 4).
one_boundary <- computeCutsIDMMAPT(
  dat_long, item_id_col = "item", rater_id_col = "Name",
  rating_col = "Kategorie", input_format = "long",
  rating_levels = level_labels, boundaries = 3.5, per_rater = FALSE
)
one_boundary$cuts_summary
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>   cut_2_3
#>     <dbl>
#> 1    488.
